questions.text: Describe the nasal cavity.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “The nasal cavity is the posterior wide part of the nose. It extends from the nostrils in front to the choanae behind, where the…” to “The nasal cavity is located between the two; orbits and below the middle part of the anterior cranial fossa. It is separated from….” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in the nasal cavity.
questions.keyConcept: The nasal cavity is the posterior wide part of the nose. It extends from the nostrils in front to the choanae behind, where the nose opens into the nasopharynx.
questions.modelAnswer:
- The nasal cavity is the posterior wide part of the nose. It extends from the nostrils in front to the choanae behind, where the nose opens into the nasopharynx.
- The nasal cavity is located between the two; orbits and below the middle part of the anterior cranial fossa. It is separated from the oral cavity below by the hard palate.
- Each nasal cavity consists of 3 general regions: nasal vestibule, respiratory region & olfactory region.
- The floor of the nasal cavity is formed of the upper surface of the palatine process of the maxilla and the horizontal plate of the palatine bone, which together form the hard palate.
- The superior & middle conchae project from the ethmoidal bone while the inferior one is a separate bone. Superior concha is the smallest while the inferior concha is the largest.
- The superior meatus is receiving the opening of the posterior ethmoidal sinuses while inferior meatus is receiving naso-lacrimal duct.
- Bulla ethmoidalis is rounded elevation produced by the middle ethmoidal sinus and open on it.
- Hiatus semi-lunaris is a deep semicircular groove below the bulla has anterior end, receives the opening of the frontal air sinus & anterior ethmoidal air sinus. And posterior end, receives the opening the maxillary air sinus.
- The lymph vessels draining the vestibule end in the submandibular nodes while the remainder of the nasal cavity is drained by vessels that pass to the upper deep cervical nodes.
- The frontal, maxillary, anterior & middle ethmoidal air sinuses all open in the middle meatus while sphenoidal opens in spheno-ethmoidal recess and posterior ethmoidal opens in superior meatus.

questions.text: Mention the sensory innervation of the external nose.
questions.explanation: This essay expects a concise nerve-by-region list rather than a detailed descriptive account, so the model answer is organized as a quick regional map: root/dorsum/tip via the ophthalmic division, ala via the maxillary division. questions.modelAnswer:
- The skin of the external nose is supplied entirely by branches of the trigeminal nerve.
- The root and upper dorsum receive the infratrochlear nerve (from the nasociliary nerve, ophthalmic division).
- The lower dorsum and tip receive the external nasal nerve, the terminal cutaneous branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve (also ophthalmic division, via the nasociliary nerve).
- The ala and lower lateral part of the nose are supplied by nasal branches of the infraorbital nerve, a branch of the maxillary division.
- In short: the ophthalmic division (infratrochlear and external nasal nerves) covers the root, dorsum, and tip, while the maxillary division (infraorbital nerve) covers the ala and lower lateral wall.

questions.text: Give an account on the sensory innervation of the external nose.
questions.explanation: Because this prompt calls for a fuller account rather than a brief list, the model answer traces the course of each nerve from its origin to its cutaneous distribution and adds a clinical correlation about differential numbness patterns and rhinoplasty risk. This depth and the added surgical relevance are what separate a 'give an account' response from the shorter 'mention' response expected in the previous essay question.
questions.keyConcept: Detailed course and clinical relevance of ophthalmic and maxillary nerve supply to the external nose
questions.modelAnswer:
- The external nose is entirely supplied by cutaneous branches of the trigeminal nerve, divided between its ophthalmic and maxillary divisions.
- From the ophthalmic division, the nasociliary nerve gives rise to two important branches: the infratrochlear nerve, which emerges near the medial canthus of the eye and supplies the skin over the root and upper part of the bridge of the nose, and the anterior ethmoidal nerve, whose terminal cutaneous continuation, the external nasal nerve, emerges between the nasal bone and the lateral nasal cartilage to supply the skin of the lower dorsum, tip, and part of the ala.
- From the maxillary division, the infraorbital nerve emerges through the infraorbital foramen on the face and sends nasal branches to supply the skin of the ala and the adjoining lateral part of the nose near the nostril.
- Clinically, this dual supply explains why a lesion of the ophthalmic division may cause numbness limited to the nasal bridge and tip while sparing the ala, whereas a maxillary division lesion has the opposite pattern.
- The external nasal nerve is also of surgical importance because it can be inadvertently injured during rhinoplasty, leading to numbness of the nasal tip.

questions.text: Describe the lateral wall of the nose.
questions.explanation: A complete description of the lateral wall must integrate three layers of information: the bones that build it, the conchae/meatus system it creates, and the specific sinus/duct openings each meatus receives, since these drainage relationships are the clinically important payoff of the bony anatomy. The model answer also folds in vascular, nerve, and lymphatic supply briefly at the end, since a thorough 'describe' question in gross anatomy typically expects these systems to be mentioned alongside the skeletal framework.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral wall = bony framework + three conchae/meatuses + specific sinus and duct openings
questions.modelAnswer:
- The lateral wall of the nasal cavity is formed by several bones from front to back and top to bottom: the nasal bone and frontal process of the maxilla anteriorly, the lacrimal bone, the ethmoid bone's lateral mass (bearing the superior and middle conchae), the inferior nasal concha (a separate bone), the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone, and the medial pterygoid plate of the sphenoid bone posteriorly.
- Three bony projections called conchae (superior, middle, and inferior) curve down from this wall, dividing the space beneath and lateral to them into three passages: the superior, middle, and inferior meatus, plus the sphenoethmoidal recess above and behind the superior concha.
- The inferior meatus, below the inferior concha, receives the opening of the nasolacrimal duct.
- The middle meatus contains the bulla ethmoidalis (formed by the middle ethmoidal air cells, onto which they open) and, just below and in front of it, the hiatus semilunaris, through which the frontal sinus and anterior ethmoidal cells drain anteriorly and the maxillary sinus drains posteriorly.
- The superior meatus receives the opening of the posterior ethmoidal air cells, while the sphenoethmoidal recess receives the opening of the sphenoidal sinus.
- The lateral wall is supplied by branches of the ophthalmic and maxillary divisions of the trigeminal nerve, and by the greater palatine, sphenopalatine, and anterior/posterior ethmoidal arteries, with lymphatic drainage passing mainly to the upper deep cervical nodes (except the vestibule, which drains to the submandibular nodes).

questions.text: A 52-year-old man, a chronic smoker, visited an ENT consultant with complaints of recurrent sinusitis, weight loss, and severe pain in the upper teeth and right half of the face. A CT scan confirmed the presence of a tumor of the maxillary air sinus.
questions.explanation: This presentation, a chronic smoking history, weight loss, facial pain, and dental pain together with a mass confirmed on imaging, is concerning for a maxillary sinus malignancy rather than simple infective sinusitis; the facial and dental pain reflect tumor involvement of the superior alveolar and infraorbital nerves that normally supply this sinus.

subQuestions.text: Where is the opening of the maxillary air sinus?

subQuestions.text: What is the nerve supply of the maxillary sinus?
subQuestions.explanation: The decisive point is “The superior alveolar nerves (anterior, middle, and posterior) and the infraorbital nerve.” This directly resolves the nerve supply of the maxillary sinus and prevents confusion with nearby structures or related diagnoses.

subQuestions.text: What is the reason that makes maxillary sinusitis very common?
subQuestions.explanation: The answer links “Because: (a) its ostium lies close to the roof rather than the floor, making drainage against gravity difficult” with “(b) discharge from an infected frontal sinus or anterior ethmoidal cells can pass into it since all three drain into the middle meatus via….” Together they supply the anatomical or clinical relationship the subquestion asks you to justify.

questions.text: An elderly man presented with severe pain beneath his left eye, radiating into the lower eyelid, the lateral side of the nose, and the upper lip.
questions.explanation: This distribution of pain, lower eyelid, lateral nose, and upper lip, corresponds precisely to the cutaneous territory of the infraorbital nerve, suggesting either infraorbital neuralgia or, given its close relationship to the maxillary sinus roof, possible maxillary sinus pathology irritating the nerve as it traverses the infraorbital canal.
questions.keyConcept: Infraorbital nerve territory and its relation to the maxillary sinus

subQuestions.text: What is the nerve that is involved in this condition?
subQuestions.explanation: The decisive point is “The infraorbital nerve.” This directly resolves the nerve that is involved in this condition and prevents confusion with nearby structures or related diagnoses.

subQuestions.text: What is the paranasal sinus closely related to this nerve?

subQuestions.keyConcept: The maxillary air sinus — the central fact needed for the paranasal sinus closely related to this nerve.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: The maxillary air sinus.

subQuestions.text: From where does this nerve originate?

subQuestions.keyConcept: It arises from the maxillary nerve (the maxillary division, V2, of the trigeminal nerve) — the central fact needed for From where does this nerve originate.

questions.text: The vocal folds extend between:
questions.explanation: Each vocal fold (vocal ligament plus overlying mucosa) stretches from the vocal process of the arytenoid cartilage posteriorly to the angle of the thyroid cartilage anteriorly, forming the free edge that vibrates during phonation.
questions.keyConcept: Vocal fold: thyroid angle to arytenoid vocal process

questions.text: The vocal folds are abducted by:
questions.explanation: The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only muscle that abducts (opens) the vocal folds by rotating the arytenoid's muscular process posteromedially, which swings the vocal process laterally; all the other listed muscles are adductors or tensors.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior cricoarytenoid = abductor

questions.text: Lesion or section of the inferior (recurrent) laryngeal nerve would paralyse the intrinsic laryngeal muscles Except:
questions.explanation: Cricothyroid is unique among laryngeal muscles in being supplied by the external laryngeal nerve (a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve), not the recurrent laryngeal nerve, so it escapes paralysis when the recurrent laryngeal nerve is damaged.
questions.keyConcept: Cricothyroid spared in recurrent laryngeal nerve injury

questions.text: The nerve beneath the mucous membrane of the piriform fossa is:
questions.explanation: The internal laryngeal nerve runs deep to the mucosa of the piriform fossa before piercing the thyrohyoid membrane, which is why a foreign body lodged there can irritate this nerve and trigger a strong cough reflex.
questions.keyConcept: Internal laryngeal nerve underlies piriform fossa mucosa

questions.text: A foreign body arrested at the piriform fossa irritates which of the following nerves?
questions.explanation: The internal laryngeal nerve lies immediately beneath the mucosa of the piriform fossa, so a lodged foreign body there directly irritates this nerve, often provoking a protective cough reflex.
questions.keyConcept: Piriform fossa foreign body irritates internal laryngeal nerve

questions.text: The structure that lies in front of the bifurcation of the trachea:
questions.explanation: The deep cardiac plexus lies immediately anterior to the tracheal bifurcation in the superior mediastinum, just below the arch of the aorta, distinguishing it from the superficial cardiac plexus which lies below the aortic arch on its left side.
questions.keyConcept: Deep cardiac plexus anterior to tracheal bifurcation

questions.text: As regards the larynx, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The larynx is covered anteriorly by the infrahyoid (strap) muscles. It actually lies opposite C3-C6 vertebrae, is related posteriorly (not anteriorly) to the esophagus, is related laterally to the thyroid gland lobes (not parathyroid), and has three single cartilages (epiglottis, thyroid, cricoid), not four.
questions.keyConcept: Laryngeal relations mnemonic: anterior = strap (infrahyoid) muscles; posterior = laryngopharynx/esophagus; lateral = thyroid lobes and carotid sheath; vertebral level C3-C6.
options: It lies infront of C2-C5 vertebra
It is related anteriorly to infrahyoid muscles
It is related anteriorly to esophagus
It is related laterally to parathyroid gland

questions.text: As regards the parts of the thyroid cartilage & the structures attached to it, choose the INCORRECT matching:
questions.explanation: The sternothyroid muscle actually attaches to the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage, not to its posterior border, making option e the incorrect matching among otherwise correct attachments.
questions.keyConcept: Sternothyroid attaches to oblique line, not posterior border
options: Inner aspect of its angle - vestibular ligament
Oblique line - inferior constrictor of pharynx

questions.text: As regards the laryngeal muscles, match each muscle in the left column with its appropriate action in right column: Cricothyroid; Posterior cricoarytenoid; Transverse arytenoid; Thyroarytenoid; Aryepiglottic muscle.
questions.explanation: Each intrinsic/external laryngeal muscle has one principal action: cricothyroid tenses the cords, posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor, transverse (interarytenoid) adducts, thyroarytenoid relaxes/shortens the cords, and the aryepiglottic muscle narrows the laryngeal inlet as a sphincter during swallowing.
questions.keyConcept: Match each premise by the specific relationship tested in “As regards the laryngeal muscles, match each muscle in the left column with its appropriate action in right…”; do not apply one rule to every pair.

questions.text: As regards relations of thoracic part of the trachea, choose the CORRECT matching:
questions.explanation: The superior vena cava lies on the right side of the trachea in the superior mediastinum. The brachiocephalic vein and arch of aorta are related anteriorly (not posteriorly), the arch of the azygos vein passes on the right side (not left), and the deep cardiac plexus lies anterior (not lateral) to the tracheal bifurcation.
questions.keyConcept: Superior vena cava lies right of trachea
options: Arch of azygos - lies on its left side
Superior vena cava - lies on its right side
Arch of aorta - is related posteriorly
Deep cardiac plexus - is related laterally

questions.text: Which one of the following vessels is most likely to be cut when doing a tracheostomy (opening the trachea from the front):
questions.explanation: The inferior thyroid veins form a venous plexus that crosses directly anterior to the lower cervical trachea before draining into the left brachiocephalic vein, putting them at risk of injury during a tracheostomy incision at that level.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior thyroid veins at risk during tracheostomy

questions.text: Describe the nerve supply of the larynx.
questions.explanation: The larynx's motor and sensory supply divides at the level of the vocal cords, with cricothyroid as the classic motor exception supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Recurrent laryngeal nerve (motor, except cricothyroid) + internal/external laryngeal nerves
questions.modelAnswer:
- Motor supply: all intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve (a branch of the vagus) EXCEPT the cricothyroid muscle, which is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve (a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, itself a branch of the vagus).
- Sensory supply: mucosa above the level of the vocal cords is supplied by the internal laryngeal nerve (a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve); mucosa below the level of the vocal cords is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
- Both the superior laryngeal nerve and recurrent laryngeal nerve are branches of the vagus nerve (CN X), so all laryngeal innervation ultimately derives from the vagus.

questions.text: Enumerate the structures attached to the thyroid cartilage.
questions.explanation: The thyroid cartilage's oblique line, posterior borders, and inner angle serve as attachment sites for extrinsic strap/pharyngeal muscles as well as intrinsic laryngeal ligaments and muscles, making it the main structural anchor of the larynx.
questions.keyConcept: Thyroid cartilage: attachment site for strap muscles, pharyngeal constrictors, and vocal ligaments
questions.modelAnswer:
Muscles/structures attached to the thyroid cartilage include:
- Thyrohyoid membrane (attached to upper border and superior horn) and thyrohyoid muscle (oblique line).
- Sternothyroid muscle (oblique line).
- Inferior constrictor of pharynx (oblique line).
- Palatopharyngeus and stylopharyngeus muscles (posterior border).
- Cricothyroid muscle and cricothyroid ligament/membrane (lower border, connecting to cricoid cartilage).
- Vestibular ligament and vocal ligament, and thyroepiglottic ligament (attached to the inner aspect of the laryngeal prominence/angle).
- Vocalis and thyroarytenoid muscles (posterior surface of the angle).

questions.text: Describe the quadrangular membrane.
questions.explanation: The quadrangular membrane is the fibroelastic sheet of the upper larynx, analogous in position to the conus elasticus below, and its two free borders directly form the aryepiglottic fold above and the vestibular ligament below.
questions.keyConcept: Quadrangular membrane: epiglottis to arytenoid, forms aryepiglottic fold (upper) and vestibular ligament (lower)
questions.modelAnswer:
- The quadrangular membrane is a submucosal sheet of fibroelastic tissue on each side of the larynx, lying beneath the mucous membrane of the laryngeal vestibule.
- Attachments: anteriorly to the lateral margin of the epiglottis; posteriorly to the anterolateral surface of the arytenoid cartilage.
- Borders: its upper (free) border thickens to form the aryepiglottic fold (containing the aryepiglottic muscle); its lower (free) border thickens to form the vestibular ligament, which underlies the vestibular (false) fold.
- Function: it helps support the vestibular folds and contributes to the framework separating the laryngeal vestibule from the laryngeal sinus/ventricle.

questions.text: A two-year-old girl filled her mouth with beads and suddenly developed continuous cough. Her mother suspected that she accidentally inhaled one of them in her airway and took her immediately to the emergency hospital.
questions.explanation: This case tests the well-known anatomical asymmetry between the right and left principal bronchi and its direct clinical relevance to foreign body aspiration.
questions.keyConcept: Right main bronchus anatomy predisposes to foreign body aspiration

subQuestions.text: To which lung would the bead go?
subQuestions.explanation: The decisive point is “The bead would most likely go to the right lung.” This directly resolves To which lung would the bead go and prevents confusion with nearby structures or related diagnoses.
subQuestions.keyConcept: The bead would most likely go to the right lung — the central fact needed for To which lung would the bead go.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: The bead would most likely go to the right lung.

subQuestions.text: Explain why.
subQuestions.explanation: The answer links “The right principal bronchus is wider in diameter, shorter in length, and runs more vertically (more in line with the long axis of the…” with “These anatomical features make aspirated foreign bodies more likely to pass into the right bronchus and lung.” Together they supply the anatomical or clinical relationship the subquestion asks you to justify.
subQuestions.keyConcept: The right principal bronchus is wider in diameter, shorter in length, and runs more vertically (more in line with the long axis of the… — the central fact needed for why.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: The right principal bronchus is wider in diameter, shorter in length, and runs more vertically (more in line with the long axis of the trachea) than the left principal bronchus, which is narrower, longer, and more oblique because it must pass beneath the arch of the aorta to reach the left lung. These anatomical features make aspirated foreign bodies more likely to pass into the right bronchus and lung.

questions.text: A four-year-old child swallowed a large metallic shirt button & began to suffocate. His parents rushed to the hospital. On doing an X-ray examination, the button was observed impacted in the larynx.
questions.explanation: This pediatric case links foreign body impaction directly to core laryngeal boundary, skeletal, and nerve-supply anatomy that determines both the obstruction and the reflex response.
questions.keyConcept: Foreign body impaction at laryngeal inlet tests inlet boundaries, cartilages, and nerve supply

subQuestions.text: Mention the boundaries of the laryngeal inlet.
subQuestions.explanation: The decisive point is “The laryngeal inlet is bounded anteriorly by the epiglottis, laterally on each side by the aryepiglottic folds, and posteriorly by the mucous membrane covering….” This directly resolves the boundaries of the laryngeal inlet and prevents confusion with nearby structures or related diagnoses.
subQuestions.keyConcept: The laryngeal inlet is bounded anteriorly by the epiglottis, laterally on each side by the aryepiglottic folds, and posteriorly by the mucous membrane covering… — the central fact needed for the boundaries of the laryngeal inlet.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: The laryngeal inlet is bounded anteriorly by the epiglottis, laterally on each side by the aryepiglottic folds, and posteriorly by the mucous membrane covering the arytenoid cartilages.

subQuestions.text: List the names of the laryngeal cartilages.
subQuestions.explanation: The answer links “Three single (unpaired) cartilages: epiglottis, thyroid cartilage, and cricoid cartilage” with “Three paired cartilages: arytenoid, corniculate, and cuneiform cartilages.” Together they supply the anatomical or clinical relationship the subquestion asks you to justify.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Three single (unpaired) cartilages: epiglottis, thyroid cartilage, and cricoid cartilage — the central fact needed for the names of the laryngeal cartilages.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Three single (unpaired) cartilages: epiglottis, thyroid cartilage, and cricoid cartilage. Three paired cartilages: arytenoid, corniculate, and cuneiform cartilages.

subQuestions.text: Mention the nerve supply of the larynx.
subQuestions.explanation: The answer links “Motor: recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic muscles except cricothyroid, which is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve” with “Sensory: internal laryngeal nerve supplies mucosa above the vocal cords.” Together they supply the anatomical or clinical relationship the subquestion asks you to justify.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Motor: recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic muscles except cricothyroid, which is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve — the central fact needed for the nerve supply of the larynx.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Motor: recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic muscles except cricothyroid, which is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve. Sensory: internal laryngeal nerve supplies mucosa above the vocal cords; recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies mucosa below the vocal cords.

questions.text: A man had metastatic carcinoma & enlarged deep cervical lymph nodes. One of his symptoms was hoarseness of voice. Subsequently he died & on doing an autopsy, it was found that one of the enlarged lymph nodes pressed on a nerve in the trachea-esophageal groove. Presumably, this was the reason for the hoarseness of voice.
questions.explanation: This case illustrates the classic clinical correlation between malignant cervical lymphadenopathy, compression of the recurrent laryngeal nerve in the tracheo-esophageal groove, and resulting vocal cord paralysis with hoarseness.
questions.keyConcept: Recurrent laryngeal nerve compression causes hoarseness

subQuestions.text: What nerve was involved?
subQuestions.explanation: The decisive point is “The (left) recurrent laryngeal nerve.” This directly resolves What nerve was involved and prevents confusion with nearby structures or related diagnoses.

subQuestions.text: What are the structures supplied by this nerve?
subQuestions.explanation: The decisive point is “The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies motor fibers to all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except cricothyroid, and sensory fibers to the laryngeal mucosa below….” This directly resolves the structures supplied by this nerve and prevents confusion with nearby structures or related diagnoses.
subQuestions.keyConcept: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies motor fibers to all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except cricothyroid, and sensory fibers to the laryngeal mucosa below… — the central fact needed for the structures supplied by this nerve.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies motor fibers to all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except cricothyroid, and sensory fibers to the laryngeal mucosa below the level of the vocal cords (it also supplies some fibers to the upper esophagus and trachea).

questions.text: As regards parts of typical ribs, match each part in the left column with its appropriate description in right column: Upper facet of head; Articular part of tubercle; Inner surface of shaft; Crest of head; Rough part of tubercle.
questions.explanation: Each part of a typical rib has a distinct articulation or ligamentous attachment: the head bears two facets (upper facet to the vertebra above, and by its crest anchors the intra-articular ligament to the disc), the tubercle bears an articular part (to the transverse process) and a rough non-articular part (for the lateral costotransverse ligament), and the inner shaft surface grooves for the neurovascular bundle.

Gives attachment to lateral costo-transverse ligament

questions.text: As regards the manubrium sterni, choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The lower border of the manubrium (at the manubriosternal joint/sternal angle) corresponds to the T4/T5 disc level, which is where the trachea bifurcates only during deep inspiration, not as a fixed correspondence; more importantly its posterior surface (not lower border directly) relates to the aortic arch, and this statement about the lower border directly corresponding to tracheal bifurcation is the intended false one among the set.
questions.keyConcept: Manubrium sterni: posterior relations and lateral rib articulations
options: Its lower border corresponds to tracheal bifurcation
Its anterior surface gives attachment to Sternohyoid muscle
Its posterior surface is related to arch of aorta
Its lateral border articulates with 2 ribs
It is related to anterior border of pleurae & lungs

questions.text: As regards the parts of the body of the sternum, match each part in the upper group with its appropriate description in the lower group: Upper end; Upper & lower parts of posterior surface of body; Median plane of posterior surface of body; Lower 1/3 of posterior surface of body; Lower left part of posterior surface of body.
questions.explanation: The sternal body's upper end forms the secondary cartilaginous manubriosternal joint, while its posterior surface has region-specific relations: the sternopericardial ligaments anchor at its upper and lower parts, the pleurae/lungs lie against its median plane, sternocostalis attaches along its lower third, and the pericardium (and heart) relates to its lower left part.
questions.keyConcept: Match each premise by the specific relationship tested in “As regards the parts of the body of the sternum, match each part in the upper group with…”; do not apply one rule to every pair.

Median plane of posterior surface of body
Lower 1/3 of posterior surface of body
Lower left part of posterior surface of body

questions.text: Match each joint in the left column with its type in the right column: Costo-vertebral joint; Joint between body of sternum & 3rd costal cartilage; Sternoclavicular joint; Manubro-sternal joint; Joint between manubrium & 1st costal cartilage.
questions.explanation: Thoracic joints show varied classifications: costovertebral and sternocostal joints (2nd rib onward) are plane synovial joints, the sternoclavicular joint is a synovial saddle joint, the manubriosternal joint is a secondary cartilaginous (symphysis) joint, and the manubrium's joint with the 1st costal cartilage is a primary cartilaginous (synchondrosis) joint since it never becomes synovial.

questions.text: Which one of the following muscles is present between the 2nd & 3rd costal cartilages?
questions.explanation: Only the internal intercostal muscle extends into the region between adjacent costal cartilages (from the sternal margin to the rib angle); the external intercostal is replaced by the anterior intercostal membrane here, and the innermost intercostal is absent in this anterior region.
questions.keyConcept: Internal intercostal muscle occupies the interchondral region

questions.text: As regards the intercostal arteries, match each artery in the left column with its artery of origin in the right column: 8th anterior I.C. artery; 2nd posterior I.C. artery; 5th anterior I.C. artery; 3rd posterior I.C. artery; Superior I.C. artery.

questions.keyConcept: Match each premise by the specific relationship tested in “As regards the intercostal arteries, match each artery in the left column with its artery of origin in…”; do not apply one rule to every pair.

questions.text: As regards the intercostal veins, match each vein in the left column with the vein in which it drains in the right column: 2nd anterior I.C. vein; 3rd right posterior I.C. vein; 5th left posterior I.C. vein; 4th left anterior I.C. vein; 1st right posterior I.C. vein.
questions.explanation: Anterior intercostal veins of the upper spaces drain into the internal thoracic vein or its accompanying venae comitantes, while posterior intercostal veins drain variably: the 1st right posterior IC vein drains directly into the right brachiocephalic vein, the 2nd-3rd right posterior IC veins form the right superior intercostal vein, and left-sided posterior IC veins from the upper spaces drain into the accessory hemiazygos vein.
questions.keyConcept: Match each premise by the specific relationship tested in “As regards the intercostal veins, match each vein in the left column with the vein in which it…”; do not apply one rule to every pair.

questions.text: As regards the major openings of the diaphragm, match each statement in the left column with its corresponding opening in the right column: Lies 1 inch to right of median plane; Lies at level of T10; Lies within central tendon; Lies within fibers of right crus; Lies behind median arcuate ligament.
questions.explanation: The three major diaphragmatic openings are distinguished by location and level: the vena caval opening lies in the central tendon about 1 inch right of the midline (~T8), the oesophageal opening lies within the muscular fibers of the right crus at T10, and the aortic opening lies posteriorly behind the median arcuate ligament at the T12 level, remaining a purely osseo-ligamentous (not muscular) opening so the aorta is never compressed by diaphragmatic contraction.

pairs.premise: Lies 1 inch to right of median plane
Lies within fibers of right crus

questions.text: Match each structure in the left column with its corresponding foramen in the right column: Subcostal vessels; Right phrenic nerve; Gastric nerves; Sympathetic trunk; Thoracic duct.
questions.explanation: Diaphragmatic passage sites are highly specific: the sympathetic trunk passes behind the medial arcuate ligament, subcostal vessels pass behind the lateral arcuate ligament, the right phrenic nerve pierces the diaphragm at (or near) the vena caval opening, the gastric (vagal) nerves pass through the oesophageal opening with the oesophagus, and the thoracic duct passes through the aortic opening along with the aorta and azygos vein.
questions.keyConcept: Match each premise by the specific relationship tested in “Match each structure in the left column with its corresponding foramen in the right column: Subcostal vessels; Right…”; do not apply one rule to every pair.

questions.text: Regarding the intercostal nerves, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The 3rd through 6th intercostal nerves are considered typical intercostal nerves, so the 4th qualifies. They supply the parietal (not visceral) pleura and pericardium, it is specifically the 2nd (not 4th) intercostal nerve's lateral cutaneous branch (intercostobrachial nerve) that supplies axillary skin, and within the costal groove the nerve lies below (not above) the intercostal vein and artery.
questions.keyConcept: 3rd-6th intercostal nerves are the typical intercostal nerves
options: The 4th intercostal nerve supplies the skin of axilla (through its lateral cutaneous branch)
Within the costal groove, they are located above intercostal arteries

questions.text: The joints of the manubrium sterni do not include:
questions.explanation: A hinge synovial joint is not among the manubrium's articulations; instead it has a saddle synovial joint (sternoclavicular), a plane synovial joint (with 2nd costal cartilage), a primary cartilaginous joint (with 1st costal cartilage), and a secondary cartilaginous joint (manubriosternal).
questions.keyConcept: Manubrium joints exclude hinge synovial type

questions.text: The second costal cartilage can be located by palpating the:
questions.explanation: The sternal angle (the palpable ridge at the manubriosternal joint, at the T4/T5 disc level) marks the point where the 2nd costal cartilage articulates with the sternum, making it the key landmark for counting ribs and intercostal spaces clinically.
questions.keyConcept: Sternal angle marks the 2nd costal cartilage level

questions.text: Regarding intercostal arteries, choose the CORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The musculophrenic artery, a terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery, supplies the anterior intercostal arteries of the 7th-9th spaces. Within the costal groove the vein (not artery) is most superior, the 1st-2nd posterior branches come from the superior intercostal artery (not aorta), collateral branches do not supply the lung, and only the upper 6 (not 8) anterior branches come directly from the internal thoracic artery.
questions.keyConcept: Musculophrenic artery supplies anterior IC arteries of 7th-9th spaces

All the posterior branches are from the aorta
The collateral branches supply the lung
The upper 8 anterior branches are from the internal thoracic artery

questions.text: When inserting a needle to obtain a sample of fluid from the pleural cavity, intercostal nerves are avoided by placing the needle:

questions.keyConcept: Thoracocentesis needle placed above upper border of rib to avoid neurovascular bundle
options: A little above upper border of rib
At posterior end of intercostal space
At anterior end of intercostal space

questions.text: Which of the following right posterior intercostal veins drains into the brachiocephalic vein?
