questions.text: Give an account on respiratory muscles and their role in the respiratory cycle.
questions.explanation: A complete response must include the distinct points represented by “Inspiratory muscles: the diaphragm is the principal muscle of inspiration (supplied by the phrenic nerve); its contraction flattens the dome and increases the vertical…” and “Expiratory muscles: quiet expiration is passive, produced by elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall as the inspiratory muscles relax. Forced expiration recruits….” Keeping both visible prevents one component from being mistaken for the whole of an account on respiratory muscles and their role in the respiratory cycle.
questions.keyConcept: Inspiratory muscles: the diaphragm is the principal muscle of inspiration (supplied by the phrenic nerve); its contraction flattens the dome and increases the vertical diameter of the thorax. The external intercostal muscles contract to elevate the ribs and push the sternum outward, increasing the transverse and antero-posterior diameters. In deep/forced inspiration, accessory muscles (sternomastoid, scalenes, alae nasi) are recruited.
questions.modelAnswer:
Inspiratory muscles: the diaphragm is the principal muscle of inspiration (supplied by the phrenic nerve); its contraction flattens the dome and increases the vertical diameter of the thorax. The external intercostal muscles contract to elevate the ribs and push the sternum outward, increasing the transverse and antero-posterior diameters. In deep/forced inspiration, accessory muscles (sternomastoid, scalenes, alae nasi) are recruited.
Expiratory muscles: quiet expiration is passive, produced by elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall as the inspiratory muscles relax. Forced expiration recruits the internal intercostal muscles (pull the ribs down and in) and the abdominal muscles (rectus abdominis, external/internal obliques, transversus abdominis), which raise intra-abdominal pressure and push the diaphragm upward.

questions.text: Describe the sequence of events that cause air to move into the lungs during inspiration and out during expiration.
questions.explanation: Breathing is driven by pressure gradients created by respiratory muscle action on thoracic volume (Boyle's law): the diaphragm and external intercostals are the principal inspiratory muscles, quiet expiration is passive (elastic recoil), and forced expiration recruits the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles; intrapleural pressure stays sub-atmospheric throughout normal breathing.
questions.keyConcept: Breathing is driven by pressure gradients created by respiratory muscle action on thoracic volume (Boyle's law): the diaphragm and external intercostals are the principal inspiratory muscles, quiet expiration is passive (elastic recoil), and forced expiration recruits the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles; intrapleural pressure stays sub-atmospheric throughout normal breathing. Exam focus: the sequence of events that cause air to move into the lungs during inspiration and out during expiration.
questions.modelAnswer:
Inspiration: inspiratory muscles (diaphragm, external intercostals) contract → thoracic cavity volume increases → intrapleural pressure becomes more negative → the lungs are pulled open and transpulmonary pressure rises → alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric pressure → air flows down the pressure gradient into the alveoli until alveolar pressure again equals atmospheric pressure.
Expiration: inspiratory muscles relax → elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall decreases thoracic volume → alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric pressure → air flows out of the lungs until the pressures equalize again. Forced expiration adds active contraction of expiratory muscles to further reduce thoracic volume.

questions.text: Define pulmonary surfactant - Discuss its function and effects of its deficiency.
questions.explanation: Lung compliance is the change in lung volume per unit change in transpulmonary pressure and reflects the distensibility of lung tissue; pulmonary surfactant (secreted by type II alveolar cells) lowers alveolar surface tension, increases compliance, reduces the work of breathing, and stabilizes alveoli of different sizes, per Laplace's law (P = 2T/r). Here it is applied specifically to Define pulmonary surfactant - Discuss its function and effects of its deficiency.
questions.keyConcept: Lung compliance is the change in lung volume per unit change in transpulmonary pressure and reflects the distensibility of lung tissue; pulmonary surfactant (secreted by type II alveolar cells) lowers alveolar surface tension, increases compliance, reduces the work of breathing, and stabilizes alveoli of different sizes, per Laplace's law (P = 2T/r). Exam focus: pulmonary surfactant - Discuss its function and effects of its deficiency.
questions.modelAnswer:
Definition: a lipoprotein (mainly dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine) secreted by type II alveolar epithelial cells that forms a monolayer at the air-liquid interface of the alveoli.
Functions: (1) lowers alveolar surface tension, increasing lung compliance and reducing the work of breathing; (2) stabilizes alveoli of different sizes by lowering tension more in small alveoli than large ones (prevents small alveoli emptying into large ones, per Laplace's law); (3) keeps alveoli relatively dry by reducing the tendency for transudation of fluid from capillaries.
Effects of deficiency: alveolar instability and collapse (atelectasis), decreased lung compliance, increased work of breathing, and tendency to pulmonary edema — classically producing (infant/neonatal) respiratory distress syndrome in premature babies.

questions.text: Explain the relation between alveolar pressure, size (radius) and surface tension in presence and in absence of pulmonary surfactant.
questions.explanation: Lung compliance is the change in lung volume per unit change in transpulmonary pressure and reflects the distensibility of lung tissue; pulmonary surfactant (secreted by type II alveolar cells) lowers alveolar surface tension, increases compliance, reduces the work of breathing, and stabilizes alveoli of different sizes, per Laplace's law (P = 2T/r). Here it is applied specifically to Explain the relation between alveolar pressure, size (radius) and surface tension in presence and in absence of pulmonary surfactant.
questions.keyConcept: Lung compliance is the change in lung volume per unit change in transpulmonary pressure and reflects the distensibility of lung tissue; pulmonary surfactant (secreted by type II alveolar cells) lowers alveolar surface tension, increases compliance, reduces the work of breathing, and stabilizes alveoli of different sizes, per Laplace's law (P = 2T/r). Exam focus: the relation between alveolar pressure, size (radius) and surface tension in presence and in absence of pulmonary surfactant.
questions.modelAnswer:
- By Laplace's law for a sphere, the collapsing pressure P = 2T/r, where T is surface tension and r is radius.
- Without surfactant, T is constant regardless of alveolar size, so small alveoli (small r) generate a much higher collapsing pressure than large alveoli for the same tension — this would make small alveoli unstable and cause them to empty into larger ones.
- Surfactant reduces surface tension, and does so proportionally more as the alveolus gets smaller (surfactant molecules become more concentrated at the smaller surface area), so T falls in step with r.
- This keeps 2T/r roughly similar across alveoli of different sizes, stabilizing alveoli of all sizes and preventing collapse of the smallest ones.

questions.text: Define lung compliance, what are the factors that affect it.
questions.explanation: Compliance is measured as ΔV/ΔP. Fibrosis, edema, congestion, and surfactant deficiency make the lung stiffer, whereas emphysema raises compliance by destroying elastic recoil.
questions.keyConcept: Lung compliance is the change in lung volume per unit change in transpulmonary pressure and reflects the distensibility of lung tissue; pulmonary surfactant (secreted by type II alveolar cells) lowers alveolar surface tension, increases compliance, reduces the work of breathing, and stabilizes alveoli of different sizes, per Laplace's law (P = 2T/r). Exam focus: lung compliance, what are the factors that affect it.
questions.modelAnswer:
Definition: lung compliance is the change in lung volume produced per unit change in transpulmonary (distending) pressure (ΔV/ΔP); it is a measure of the distensibility/elasticity of lung tissue — the reciprocal of elastance.
Factors affecting it: amount of elastic tissue (collagen and elastin) in the lung; amount of pulmonary surfactant (surfactant increases compliance); pulmonary blood volume/congestion (congestion decreases compliance); presence of fibrosis (decreases compliance) or emphysema (increases compliance due to loss of elastic tissue); lung volume/region of the pressure-volume curve at which compliance is measured; age and posture.

questions.text: Draw a labeled diagram representing the different lung volumes. Describe the factors affecting the vital capacity.
questions.explanation: Lung volumes (tidal volume, inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes, residual volume) combine into capacities (vital capacity, inspiratory capacity, functional residual capacity, total lung capacity); volumes that include the residual volume (FRC, TLC, RV) cannot be measured directly by simple spirometry and require a dilution or plethysmography method.
questions.keyConcept: Lung volumes (tidal volume, inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes, residual volume) combine into capacities (vital capacity, inspiratory capacity, functional residual capacity, total lung capacity); volumes that include the residual volume (FRC, TLC, RV) cannot be measured directly by simple spirometry and require a dilution or plethysmography method. Exam focus: Draw a labeled diagram representing the different lung volumes. Describe the factors affecting the vital capacity.
questions.modelAnswer:
Lung volumes (from largest lung state to smallest): Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV), Tidal Volume (TV), Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV), and Residual Volume (RV) remaining after maximal expiration. Capacities are combinations: Inspiratory Capacity = IRV + TV; Functional Residual Capacity = ERV + RV; Vital Capacity = IRV + TV + ERV; Total Lung Capacity = Vital Capacity + RV.
Factors affecting vital capacity: body size and height, sex (lower in females), age (decreases with advancing age), body position (greater when standing than supine), strength of the respiratory muscles, compliance of the lungs and chest wall, pregnancy (reduced in late pregnancy due to diaphragm elevation), and restrictive or obstructive lung disease.

questions.text: Define "Dead space" and mention its types, describe one method for measurement of dead space.
questions.explanation: The model answer should be read as a causal or classificatory chain for “Define "Dead space" and mention its types, describe one method for measurement of dead space”: identify the defining variable first, then use its downstream consequence to distinguish the concept from neighboring respiratory mechanisms.
questions.keyConcept: Physiological dead space is the portion of tidal volume that does not participate in gas exchange (anatomical dead space in the conducting airways plus any under-perfused alveoli); alveolar ventilation equals respiratory rate times (tidal volume minus dead space), and the ventilation/perfusion ratio varies from apex (high V/Q) to base (low V/Q) of the upright lung.
questions.modelAnswer:
Definition: dead space is the volume of inspired air that does not take part in gas exchange.
Types: (1) Anatomical dead space — volume of the conducting airways from nose/mouth to the terminal bronchioles (about 150 ml); (2) Alveolar dead space — volume of ventilated alveoli that are not adequately perfused; Physiological dead space = anatomical + alveolar dead space (approximately equal to anatomical dead space in the healthy lung).
Measurement: Fowler's nitrogen washout method (single-breath, measures anatomical dead space from the volume expired before the abrupt rise in expired nitrogen concentration) and Bohr's method using CO2 (measures physiological dead space): VD = VT × (PaCO2 − PēCO2) / PaCO2, where PēCO2 is mixed expired CO2 tension.

questions.text: Discuss the structure of the respiratory membrane. What are the factors which affect gas diffusion through it.
questions.explanation: The membrane is efficient because type I epithelium, fused basal laminae, and capillary endothelium create a very short path. Disease impairs diffusion by reducing area, increasing thickness, or reducing the partial-pressure gradient.
questions.keyConcept: Gas diffusion across the respiratory membrane follows Fick's law: it is directly proportional to surface area, the partial-pressure gradient, and gas solubility, and inversely proportional to membrane thickness and the square root of molecular weight. Exam focus: the structure of the respiratory membrane. What are the factors which affect gas diffusion through it.
questions.modelAnswer:
Structure (layers, from alveolar air to capillary blood): a thin fluid layer containing surfactant; the alveolar epithelium (mainly type I pneumocytes) and its basement membrane; a thin interstitial space; the capillary basement membrane; and the capillary endothelium. Total thickness is about 0.2–0.6 micron in places, allowing rapid diffusion.
Factors affecting diffusion (Fick's law): membrane thickness (diffusion rate is inversely proportional), total surface area available, the diffusion coefficient/solubility of the gas (CO2 diffuses about 20 times faster than O2), the partial-pressure gradient of the gas across the membrane, and the molecular weight of the gas (diffusion is inversely proportional to the square root of molecular weight).

questions.text: Discuss the transport of O2 by the blood.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “Oxygen is carried in the blood in two forms: (1) physically dissolved in plasma (a small fraction, about 1.5% of total O2 content, following…” to “Each hemoglobin molecule can bind up to four O2 molecules; binding is cooperative, so binding of the first O2 increases the affinity for subsequent….” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in the transport of O2 by the blood.
questions.keyConcept: Exam focus — the transport of O2 by the blood: Oxygen is carried in the blood in two forms: (1) physically dissolved in plasma (a small fraction, about 1.5% of total O2 content, following Henry's law), and (2) chemically combined….
questions.modelAnswer:
- Oxygen is carried in the blood in two forms: (1) physically dissolved in plasma (a small fraction, about 1.5% of total O2 content, following Henry's law), and (2) chemically combined with hemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin (about 98.5% of total O2 content).
- Each hemoglobin molecule can bind up to four O2 molecules; binding is cooperative, so binding of the first O2 increases the affinity for subsequent molecules, producing the sigmoid O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve.
- O2 is loaded onto hemoglobin in the pulmonary capillaries (high PO2) and unloaded to the tissues (low PO2), with the amount unloaded depending on the tissue's metabolic demand and the position/shift of the dissociation curve.

questions.text: Draw a labeled diagram representing the O2 hemoglobin dissociation curve & factors affecting it.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “The O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve is sigmoid, plotting percentage hemoglobin saturation (y-axis) against PO2 (x-axis); P50 (the PO2 at 50% saturation) is normally about 26-27…” to “Factors shifting the curve to the right (decreased Hb affinity for O2, easier unloading to tissues): increased temperature, increased PCO2/H+ (Bohr effect), increased 2,3-diphosphoglycerate….” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in Draw a labeled diagram representing the O2 hemoglobin dissociation curve & factors affecting it.
questions.keyConcept: The O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve is sigmoid, plotting percentage hemoglobin saturation (y-axis) against PO2 (x-axis); P50 (the PO2 at 50% saturation) is normally about 26-27 mmHg. It has a flat upper part (PO2 60-100 mmHg, corresponding to the lungs) and a steep lower part (PO2 below about 40 mmHg, corresponding to the tissues).
questions.modelAnswer:
The O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve is sigmoid, plotting percentage hemoglobin saturation (y-axis) against PO2 (x-axis); P50 (the PO2 at 50% saturation) is normally about 26-27 mmHg. It has a flat upper part (PO2 60-100 mmHg, corresponding to the lungs) and a steep lower part (PO2 below about 40 mmHg, corresponding to the tissues).
Factors shifting the curve to the right (decreased Hb affinity for O2, easier unloading to tissues): increased temperature, increased PCO2/H+ (Bohr effect), increased 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG), and exercise. Factors shifting the curve to the left (increased affinity): decreased temperature, decreased PCO2/H+, decreased 2,3-DPG, fetal hemoglobin, and carbon monoxide (which also reduces O2 capacity).

questions.text: Describe the O2 hemoglobin dissociation curve-mention the cause of its shift to the right.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “The O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve is a sigmoid relationship between PO2 and percentage hemoglobin saturation, with a flat upper portion around the normal arterial PO2…” to “A rightward shift lowers the affinity of hemoglobin for O2 (increased P50), favoring O2 release to the tissues, and is caused by: increased temperature,….” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in the O2 hemoglobin dissociation curve-mention the cause of its shift to the right.
questions.keyConcept: Exam focus — the O2 hemoglobin dissociation curve-mention the cause of its shift to the right: The O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve is a sigmoid relationship between PO2 and percentage hemoglobin saturation, with a flat upper portion around the normal arterial PO2 range and a steep lower portion….
questions.modelAnswer:
- The O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve is a sigmoid relationship between PO2 and percentage hemoglobin saturation, with a flat upper portion around the normal arterial PO2 range and a steep lower portion at the low PO2 levels found in actively metabolizing tissue.
- A rightward shift lowers the affinity of hemoglobin for O2 (increased P50), favoring O2 release to the tissues, and is caused by: increased temperature, increased PCO2 and H+ concentration (the Bohr effect, as occurs with metabolically active/acidotic tissue), increased 2,3-DPG (as in chronic hypoxia or high-altitude acclimatization), and exercise.

questions.text: Draw the O2 hemoglobin dissociation curve and explain the significance of upper flat part and lower steep part of the curve.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “Upper flat part (PO2 approximately 60-100 mmHg): hemoglobin saturation changes very little even with fairly large changes in PO2. This provides a safety margin…” to “Lower steep part (PO2 below about 40 mmHg, the range found in tissue capillaries): a small further fall in PO2 causes a large fall….” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in Draw the O2 hemoglobin dissociation curve and explain the significance of upper flat part and lower steep part of the curve.
questions.keyConcept: Upper flat part (PO2 approximately 60-100 mmHg): hemoglobin saturation changes very little even with fairly large changes in PO2. This provides a safety margin for O2 loading in the lungs — saturation stays high (>90%) even if alveolar PO2 falls somewhat (e.g., with mild lung disease or moderate altitude).
questions.modelAnswer:
Upper flat part (PO2 approximately 60-100 mmHg): hemoglobin saturation changes very little even with fairly large changes in PO2. This provides a safety margin for O2 loading in the lungs — saturation stays high (>90%) even if alveolar PO2 falls somewhat (e.g., with mild lung disease or moderate altitude).
Lower steep part (PO2 below about 40 mmHg, the range found in tissue capillaries): a small further fall in PO2 causes a large fall in % saturation, i.e., a large amount of O2 is released. This facilitates efficient O2 unloading to metabolically active tissues, and allows more O2 to be released when tissue PO2 falls further during increased activity.

questions.text: Give an account on CO2 transport in blood and buffering of tidal CO2.
questions.explanation: A complete response must include the distinct points represented by “CO2 is transported in three forms: (1) physically dissolved in plasma (~7% of the CO2 added to blood in the tissues); (2) as bicarbonate…” and “Buffering: the H+ generated by carbonic acid dissociation is buffered mainly by hemoglobin (reduced/deoxygenated hemoglobin is a better buffer for H+ than oxygenated hemoglobin….” Keeping both visible prevents one component from being mistaken for the whole of an account on CO2 transport in blood and buffering of tidal CO2.
questions.keyConcept: CO2 is transported in three forms: (1) physically dissolved in plasma (~7% of the CO2 added to blood in the tissues); (2) as bicarbonate (~70%) — CO2 diffuses into red cells, where carbonic anhydrase rapidly converts it (with water) to carbonic acid, which dissociates into H+ and HCO3-; and (3) as carbaminohemoglobin (~23%), bound directly to the globin chains of hemoglobin.
questions.modelAnswer:
CO2 is transported in three forms: (1) physically dissolved in plasma (~7% of the CO2 added to blood in the tissues); (2) as bicarbonate (~70%) — CO2 diffuses into red cells, where carbonic anhydrase rapidly converts it (with water) to carbonic acid, which dissociates into H+ and HCO3-; and (3) as carbaminohemoglobin (~23%), bound directly to the globin chains of hemoglobin.
Buffering: the H+ generated by carbonic acid dissociation is buffered mainly by hemoglobin (reduced/deoxygenated hemoglobin is a better buffer for H+ than oxygenated hemoglobin — part of the Haldane effect), preventing a large fall in blood pH as CO2 is loaded in the tissues; HCO3- diffuses out of the red cell into plasma for transport, being exchanged for chloride (chloride shift) to maintain electroneutrality.

questions.text: Explain the chloride shift phenomenon and its importance.
questions.explanation: CO2 is transported mainly as plasma bicarbonate (~70%, generated by carbonic anhydrase in red cells), as carbaminohemoglobin (~23%), and dissolved in plasma (~7%); the chloride shift maintains electroneutrality as bicarbonate leaves the red cell.
questions.keyConcept: CO2 is transported mainly as plasma bicarbonate (~70%, generated by carbonic anhydrase in red cells), as carbaminohemoglobin (~23%), and dissolved in plasma (~7%); the chloride shift maintains electroneutrality as bicarbonate leaves the red cell. Exam focus: the chloride shift phenomenon and its importance.
questions.modelAnswer:
- As CO2 enters red blood cells in the tissues, carbonic anhydrase converts it to H2CO3, which dissociates into H+ (buffered by hemoglobin) and HCO3-.
- The HCO3- diffuses out of the red cell into the plasma along its concentration gradient (this is where most CO2 is carried).
- To maintain electrical neutrality inside the cell as the negatively charged bicarbonate leaves, chloride ions (Cl-) move from plasma into the red cell via the band 3 anion exchanger — this exchange is the chloride shift.
- The reverse occurs in the pulmonary capillaries as CO2 is released.
- Importance: it allows large quantities of CO2 to be transported as plasma bicarbonate without disturbing the electrical and osmotic balance of the red blood cell.

questions.text: Describe the role of chemoreceptors in regulation of respiration.
questions.explanation: Central receptors provide most of the sustained CO₂ response through CSF H⁺, whereas carotid and aortic bodies act rapidly and become crucial in severe hypoxemia or metabolic acidosis.
questions.keyConcept: Ventilation is regulated by the medullary respiratory centres, which are driven mainly by central chemoreceptors (CO2/H+ in brain ECF, ~80% of the CO2 response) and peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic bodies, mainly sensitive to a fall in arterial PO2 below ~60 mmHg, with a rapid secondary response to CO2/H+). Exam focus: the role of chemoreceptors in regulation of respiration.
questions.modelAnswer:
Central chemoreceptors are located near the ventral surface of the medulla, bathed by CSF/brain extracellular fluid. They respond to a rise in H+ concentration in the CSF, which results from CO2 diffusing across the blood-brain barrier and being hydrated to carbonic acid; they are responsible for about 70-80% of the ventilatory response to a rise in arterial PCO2, though they respond slowly (minutes) because CO2 must diffuse across the barrier.
Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies and aortic bodies) respond mainly to a fall in arterial PO2 (significant only below about 60 mmHg) and act rapidly; they also respond, more weakly and more rapidly than central chemoreceptors, to a rise in arterial PCO2 and H+ — this is particularly important in metabolic acidosis, since H+ cannot easily cross the blood-brain barrier to stimulate central chemoreceptors directly.

questions.text: Describe briefly the non-chemical factors in control of respiration.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “Cortical (voluntary) control permits breath-holding, voluntary hyperventilation, speech, and singing” to “Pulmonary stretch receptors mediate the Hering–Breuer inflation reflex.” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in briefly the non-chemical factors in control of respiration.
questions.keyConcept: Exam focus — briefly the non-chemical factors in control of respiration: Non-chemical factors affecting respiration include: cortical (voluntary) control, allowing breath-holding or voluntary hyperventilation and speech; pulmonary stretch receptors (Hering-Breuer reflex), which inhibit further inspiration when the lungs are over-distended; irritant….
questions.modelAnswer:
- Cortical (voluntary) control permits breath-holding, voluntary hyperventilation, speech, and singing.
- Pulmonary stretch receptors mediate the Hering–Breuer inflation reflex.
- Airway irritant receptors trigger cough and bronchoconstriction.
- Juxtacapillary (J) receptors produce rapid shallow breathing and dyspnea when stimulated, as in pulmonary congestion.
- Proprioceptors from exercising muscles and joints contribute to the immediate rise in ventilation at exercise onset.
- Baroreceptor input, body temperature, emotion, and pain can also modify breathing.

questions.text: Discuss the role of the vagus nerve in the regulation of respiration.
questions.explanation: Vagal afferents carry stretch- and irritant-receptor signals to the brainstem, limiting overinflation and coordinating protective cough and bronchoconstrictor reflexes.
questions.keyConcept: Ventilation is regulated by the medullary respiratory centres, which are driven mainly by central chemoreceptors (CO2/H+ in brain ECF, ~80% of the CO2 response) and peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic bodies, mainly sensitive to a fall in arterial PO2 below ~60 mmHg, with a rapid secondary response to CO2/H+). Exam focus: the role of the vagus nerve in the regulation of respiration.
questions.modelAnswer:
- The vagus nerve carries several important respiratory afferents to the medulla: from pulmonary stretch receptors (mediating the Hering-Breuer inflation reflex, which inhibits inspiration when the lung is sufficiently inflated, and a deflation reflex that promotes inspiration when the lung deflates); from airway irritant receptors (triggering bronchoconstriction, cough, and mucus secretion in response to irritants); from juxtacapillary (J) receptors (producing rapid shallow breathing and the sensation of dyspnea, e.g., in pulmonary edema); and from the aortic body peripheral chemoreceptors and baroreceptors.
- Through these afferents the vagus helps set the depth and rate of breathing and protects the airway.

questions.text: Describe the chemical control of respiration.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “Chemical control of respiration operates through central and peripheral chemoreceptors” to “Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond to H+ generated in brain ECF/CSF from CO2 and are responsible for the majority (about 70-80%) of the….” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in the chemical control of respiration.
questions.keyConcept: Exam focus — the chemical control of respiration: Chemical control of respiration operates through central and peripheral chemoreceptors. Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond to H+ generated in brain ECF/CSF from CO2 and are responsible for the majority….
questions.modelAnswer:
- Chemical control of respiration operates through central and peripheral chemoreceptors.
- Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond to H+ generated in brain ECF/CSF from CO2 and are responsible for the majority (about 70-80%) of the response to a rise in arterial PCO2, which is normally the most potent chemical regulator of ventilation minute-to-minute.
- Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic bodies) respond mainly to a fall in arterial PO2 below about 60 mmHg (becoming the dominant drive in severe hypoxemia or chronic lung disease with CO2 retention), and also respond rapidly to increases in arterial PCO2 and H+, which is especially important in metabolic acidosis, since H+ does not readily cross the blood-brain barrier to act on central chemoreceptors directly.

questions.text: Define hypoxia, what are its types, causes and characters.
questions.explanation: Classify hypoxia by locating the failed step: arterial oxygenation, hemoglobin carriage, tissue perfusion, or cellular utilization. That framework predicts PaO₂, oxygen content, venous extraction, and response to oxygen therapy.
questions.keyConcept: Hypoxia is classified as hypoxic, anemic, circulatory (stagnant), or histotoxic hypoxia depending on whether the defect is in arterial PO2, O2-carrying capacity, blood flow, or tissue O2 utilization; acclimatization to altitude involves hyperventilation, polycythemia, and a rightward shift of the O2-Hb curve via increased 2,3-DPG. Exam focus: hypoxia, what are its types, causes and characters.
questions.modelAnswer:
Definition: hypoxia is a deficiency of oxygen at the tissue level.
Types and causes: (1) Hypoxic hypoxia — low arterial PO2, due to high altitude, hypoventilation, or lung disease (diffusion impairment, V/Q mismatch); (2) Anemic hypoxia — decreased O2-carrying capacity of blood with normal arterial PO2, due to anemia or carbon monoxide poisoning; (3) Circulatory (stagnant) hypoxia — normal arterial PO2 and O2 content but inadequate blood flow/delivery to tissues, due to heart failure, shock, or local vascular obstruction; (4) Histotoxic hypoxia — normal O2 delivery but tissues are unable to utilize O2, as in cyanide poisoning, which blocks cytochrome oxidase.
Characters: cyanosis (bluish discoloration) is typically present in hypoxic and circulatory hypoxia and in some anemic hypoxia, but is characteristically absent in severe anemia (too little total hemoglobin to show as visibly blue) and in histotoxic hypoxia/CO poisoning (skin may appear pink or cherry-red instead).

questions.text: What are the mechanisms of acclimatization to high altitudes.
questions.explanation: The adaptations occur on different timescales: immediate hyperventilation, renal bicarbonate loss over days, erythropoiesis and 2,3-DPG elevation, then longer-term vascular and cellular remodeling.
questions.keyConcept: Hypoxia is classified as hypoxic, anemic, circulatory (stagnant), or histotoxic hypoxia depending on whether the defect is in arterial PO2, O2-carrying capacity, blood flow, or tissue O2 utilization; acclimatization to altitude involves hyperventilation, polycythemia, and a rightward shift of the O2-Hb curve via increased 2,3-DPG. Exam focus: are the mechanisms of acclimatization to high altitudes.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Increased ventilation driven by peripheral chemoreceptor response to hypoxia.
- Renal bicarbonate excretion, which compensates for respiratory alkalosis and permits sustained hyperventilation.
- Increased erythropoietin, red-cell mass, and hemoglobin concentration.
- Increased 2,3-DPG, facilitating oxygen unloading to tissues.
- Increased tissue capillary density and adaptive cellular changes that improve oxygen use.
- An early rise in cardiac output that tends back toward baseline as other adaptations develop.

questions.text: Define the term hypoxia and cyanosis - Describe the types of hypoxia associated with cyanosis.
questions.explanation: Cyanosis depends on the absolute concentration of reduced hemoglobin, so it is common in hypoxic and stagnant states but may be absent in severe anemia, carbon-monoxide poisoning, and histotoxic hypoxia.
questions.keyConcept: Hypoxia is classified as hypoxic, anemic, circulatory (stagnant), or histotoxic hypoxia depending on whether the defect is in arterial PO2, O2-carrying capacity, blood flow, or tissue O2 utilization; acclimatization to altitude involves hyperventilation, polycythemia, and a rightward shift of the O2-Hb curve via increased 2,3-DPG. Exam focus: the term hypoxia and cyanosis - Describe the types of hypoxia associated with cyanosis.
questions.modelAnswer:
Hypoxia is a deficiency of O2 at the tissue level. Cyanosis is a bluish discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes caused by an increased absolute amount of deoxygenated (reduced) hemoglobin in the capillary blood (classically >5 g/dl).
Cyanosis is typically seen in hypoxic hypoxia (e.g., lung disease, high altitude) and in circulatory (stagnant) hypoxia (e.g., heart failure, local vascular obstruction), and can be seen in anemic hypoxia if there is still sufficient total hemoglobin to allow enough reduced hemoglobin to accumulate. Cyanosis is classically absent in severe anemia (insufficient total hemoglobin to produce visible cyanosis even though tissue hypoxia is present) and in histotoxic hypoxia such as cyanide poisoning or carbon monoxide poisoning, where the skin may appear pink or cherry-red despite significant tissue hypoxia.

questions.text: What are the effects of muscular exercise on respiration.
questions.explanation: Neural feed-forward raises ventilation immediately; metabolic CO₂, H⁺, and heat then sustain it. Increased perfusion and capillary recruitment raise diffusing capacity while arterial gases remain near normal in moderate exercise.
questions.keyConcept: Beyond gas exchange, the lung performs metabolic/endocrine functions (e.g., ACE-mediated activation of angiotensin I and inactivation of vasoactive peptides, surfactant and prostaglandin synthesis) and ventilation increases markedly with exercise to match the rise in O2 consumption and CO2 production. Exam focus: are the effects of muscular exercise on respiration.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Exercise produces a marked increase in pulmonary ventilation (both rate and depth), roughly matching the rise in O2 consumption and CO2 production.
- Pulmonary blood flow increases and becomes more evenly distributed (improving V/Q matching), and pulmonary diffusing capacity increases due to recruitment of additional pulmonary capillaries.
- In mild-to-moderate exercise, arterial PO2 and PCO2 change very little because ventilation is closely matched to metabolic needs; the immediate rise in ventilation at the start of exercise is driven mainly by neurogenic/proprioceptive input from exercising muscles and joints and cortical anticipatory signals, while chemical factors (CO2, H+, temperature) sustain and fine-tune ventilation during continued exercise.
- Tissue O2 extraction increases (widened arteriovenous O2 difference), and in heavy/exhaustive exercise arterial PCO2 may rise and pH may fall as lactic acidosis develops.

questions.text: In addition to providing for gas exchange, what are the other functions of the respiratory system.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “Regulation of acid–base balance through CO₂ elimination” to “Phonation and speech through airflow across the vocal folds.” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in In addition to providing for gas exchange, what are the other functions of the respiratory system.
questions.keyConcept: Exam focus — In addition to providing for gas exchange, what are the other functions of the respiratory system: Besides gas exchange, the respiratory system: helps regulate acid-base balance by controlling the rate of CO2 elimination (and hence carbonic acid/H+) from the blood; contributes to phonation and speech, as….
questions.modelAnswer:
- Regulation of acid–base balance through CO₂ elimination.
- Phonation and speech through airflow across the vocal folds.
- Airway defense through mucociliary clearance, cough, and alveolar macrophages.
- Metabolic/endocrine functions, including ACE-mediated angiotensin I activation and inactivation or synthesis of selected vasoactive substances.
- Olfaction through nasal olfactory epithelium.
- Heat and water loss through expired air.
- Reservoir and filtering functions within the pulmonary circulation.

questions.text: Describe the mechanics of ventilation.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “Ventilation depends on Boyle's law: at constant temperature, gas pressure varies inversely with volume” to “Contraction of the inspiratory muscles (diaphragm, external intercostals) increases thoracic volume, which lowers intrapleural and then alveolar pressure below atmospheric, so air flows into….” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in the mechanics of ventilation.
questions.keyConcept: Exam focus — the mechanics of ventilation: Ventilation depends on Boyle's law: at constant temperature, gas pressure varies inversely with volume. Contraction of the inspiratory muscles (diaphragm, external intercostals) increases thoracic volume, which lowers intrapleural and then….
questions.modelAnswer:
- Ventilation depends on Boyle's law: at constant temperature, gas pressure varies inversely with volume.
- Contraction of the inspiratory muscles (diaphragm, external intercostals) increases thoracic volume, which lowers intrapleural and then alveolar pressure below atmospheric, so air flows into the lungs down the pressure gradient; relaxation of these muscles (with elastic recoil of lung and chest wall) reduces thoracic volume, raising alveolar pressure above atmospheric so air flows out.
- Throughout the cycle, intrapleural pressure remains sub-atmospheric (more negative during inspiration than expiration), keeping the lungs adherent to the chest wall.
- The ease and rate of these volume changes are determined by lung and chest wall compliance (distensibility, aided by surfactant) and airway resistance (mainly in medium-sized bronchi), while elastic recoil restores the resting position during quiet expiration.

questions.text: What factors influence the amount of gas exchange occurring at the respiratory membrane?
questions.explanation: Gas diffusion across the respiratory membrane follows Fick's law: it is directly proportional to surface area, the partial-pressure gradient, and gas solubility, and inversely proportional to membrane thickness and the square root of molecular weight. Here it is applied specifically to What factors influence the amount of gas exchange occurring at the respiratory membrane.
questions.keyConcept: Gas diffusion across the respiratory membrane follows Fick's law: it is directly proportional to surface area, the partial-pressure gradient, and gas solubility, and inversely proportional to membrane thickness and the square root of molecular weight. Exam focus: factors influence the amount of gas exchange occurring at the respiratory membrane.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Surface area available for diffusion: reduced by emphysema or lung resection.
- Membrane thickness: increased by fibrosis or edema, slowing diffusion.
- Partial-pressure gradient between alveolar gas and pulmonary capillary blood.
- Gas diffusion coefficient, determined largely by solubility and molecular weight; CO₂ diffuses much faster than O₂.
- Ventilation–perfusion matching and pulmonary capillary transit time.
- Hemoglobin concentration, which influences effective O₂ uptake after diffusion.

questions.text: Describe how hemoglobin's saturation behavior varies.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “The percentage saturation of hemoglobin with O2 is a sigmoid (S-shaped) function of PO2 — the O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve — rather than a straight…” to “The curve has a flat upper portion at the PO2 range found in the lungs (60-100 mmHg), where saturation stays high (>90%) despite fairly….” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in how hemoglobin's saturation behavior varies.
questions.keyConcept: Exam focus — how hemoglobin's saturation behavior varies: The percentage saturation of hemoglobin with O2 is a sigmoid (S-shaped) function of PO2 — the O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve — rather than a straight line, because binding of O2 to….
questions.modelAnswer:
- The percentage saturation of hemoglobin with O2 is a sigmoid (S-shaped) function of PO2 — the O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve — rather than a straight line, because binding of O2 to one of hemoglobin's four heme sites increases the affinity of the remaining sites for O2 (positive cooperativity).
- The curve has a flat upper portion at the PO2 range found in the lungs (60-100 mmHg), where saturation stays high (>90%) despite fairly large changes in PO2, and a steep lower portion at the low PO2 found in tissues, where small drops in PO2 cause large releases of O2.
- The position of the curve (P50) shifts right (lower affinity, easier unloading) with increased temperature, PCO2/H+, and 2,3-DPG, and shifts left (higher affinity) with the opposite changes and with fetal hemoglobin.

questions.text: How are respiratory events regulated?
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “Basic rhythmic breathing is generated by a central pattern generator in the medulla (dorsal and ventral respiratory groups), which sets the automatic inspiratory/expiratory rhythm;…” to “This automatic drive is continuously adjusted by: central chemoreceptors (responding to CO2/H+ in brain ECF); peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies (responding….” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in are respiratory events regulated.
questions.keyConcept: Exam focus — are respiratory events regulated: Basic rhythmic breathing is generated by a central pattern generator in the medulla (dorsal and ventral respiratory groups), which sets the automatic inspiratory/expiratory rhythm; pontine centers (pneumotaxic and apneustic centers)….
questions.modelAnswer:
- Basic rhythmic breathing is generated by a central pattern generator in the medulla (dorsal and ventral respiratory groups), which sets the automatic inspiratory/expiratory rhythm; pontine centers (pneumotaxic and apneustic centers) modulate the rate and depth of this rhythm.
- This automatic drive is continuously adjusted by: central chemoreceptors (responding to CO2/H+ in brain ECF); peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies (responding mainly to falls in arterial PO2, and secondarily to CO2/H+); mechanical feedback from pulmonary stretch receptors (Hering-Breuer reflex) and irritant/J receptors carried by the vagus; input from higher centers allowing voluntary control (cortex) and emotional influences (limbic system); and other reflex inputs such as baroreceptors, temperature, and proprioceptive signals from exercising muscles.

questions.text: Define pulmonary surfactant and its mechanism of action.
questions.explanation: Surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension, which is what keeps small alveoli from collapsing (per Laplace's law) and lowers the work of breathing; its deficiency is the cause of infant respiratory distress syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Surfactant is a phospholipid-protein complex that lowers alveolar surface tension by 2- to 10-fold, which is what prevents small alveoli from collapsing.
questions.modelAnswer:
- It is a complex mixture of phospholipids, proteins, and calcium ions.
- Surfactant forms a layer between the fluid lining the alveoli and the air in the alveoli, decreasing the surface tension in the alveoli (2- to 10-fold), which plays a major role in preventing alveolar collapse.

questions.text: List the factors that shift the O₂-Hb dissociation curve to the right.
questions.explanation: This rightward shift is exactly what happens in actively metabolizing tissue (more CO2, acid, heat), so hemoglobin conveniently releases more O2 precisely where it is needed most.
questions.keyConcept: A rightward shift of the O₂-Hb curve (higher PCO₂, H+, temperature, or 2,3-DPG) lowers hemoglobin's affinity for O₂, favoring O₂ release to the tissues.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Increased blood PCO₂.
- Increased blood H+ concentration (decreased blood pH).
- Increased blood temperature.
- Increased concentration of 2,3-DPG.

questions.text: Discuss voluntary control of respiration.
questions.explanation: This cortical override pathway explains why breathing can be consciously controlled at all, in contrast to the fully automatic brainstem control that governs breathing during sleep or unconsciousness.
questions.keyConcept: Voluntary breathing bypasses the automatic brainstem rhythm generator via a direct corticospinal pathway to the respiratory motor neurons, allowing conscious override during speech or breath-holding.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Voluntary control of respiration is mediated by a pathway from the cerebral cortex to the motor neurons in the spinal cord that supply the respiratory muscles.
- Voluntary control of respiration occurs, for example, during speech, voluntary hyperventilation, or voluntary apnea (breath holding).

questions.text: Discuss the cough reflex.
questions.explanation: The cough reflex is a protective mechanism that clears the airway of irritants and secretions via this coordinated deep inspiration, glottic closure, and forced expiration.
questions.keyConcept: The cough reflex works by building high intrapulmonary pressure against a closed glottis, then suddenly releasing it, so the resulting explosive airflow physically ejects the irritant.
questions.modelAnswer:
- It starts by a sharp deep inspiration followed by forced expiration against a closed glottis; thus, the intrapulmonary pressure rises markedly.
- Then, the glottis suddenly opens, producing an explosive outflow of air, ejecting any foreign object in the air passages.

questions.text: Define histotoxic hypoxia.
questions.explanation: This distinction explains why giving more oxygen alone is often ineffective: the block is in cellular oxidative metabolism, classically cytochrome oxidase inhibition by cyanide.
questions.keyConcept: Histotoxic hypoxia is failure of cellular oxygen utilization, not failure of oxygen delivery.
questions.modelAnswer: Histotoxic hypoxia is a condition in which arterial PO₂ and oxygen content are adequate, but tissue cells cannot utilize delivered oxygen.

questions.text: What are the causes of histotoxic hypoxia?
questions.explanation: Both causes prevent cells from converting delivered oxygen into usable aerobic energy, despite normal oxygen reaching the tissues.
questions.keyConcept: Histotoxic hypoxia is caused by inhibition of cellular oxidative enzymes or essential metabolic cofactors.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Cyanide poisoning, which inhibits cytochrome c oxidase.
- Severe thiamine deficiency, which impairs oxidative metabolism.

questions.text: Define cyanosis.
questions.explanation: This is why cyanosis may be hard to detect in severe anemia and prominent in polycythemia at the same oxygen saturation.
questions.keyConcept: Cyanosis reflects the absolute amount of reduced hemoglobin, not simply a low oxygen saturation.
questions.modelAnswer: Cyanosis is a bluish discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes caused by an increased concentration of reduced (deoxygenated) hemoglobin in capillary blood, classically about 5 g/dL or more.

questions.text: What is the effect of the limbic system on respiration?
questions.explanation: This pathway explains hyperventilation during anxiety and irregular breathing during strong emotional states even without a primary blood-gas abnormality.
questions.keyConcept: Emotion can alter the automatic breathing pattern through limbic–hypothalamic control.
questions.modelAnswer: The limbic system modifies breathing during emotion, pain, fear, anxiety, and arousal through projections to hypothalamic and brainstem respiratory centers.

questions.text: Mention the importance of the cerebral cortex in ventilation.
questions.explanation: The override is limited because rising CO₂ and H⁺ eventually activate automatic respiratory drive strongly enough to restore breathing.
questions.keyConcept: The cortex can temporarily override the automatic brainstem respiratory pattern.
questions.modelAnswer: The cerebral cortex provides voluntary control of breathing through corticospinal pathways to respiratory motor neurons, enabling speech, singing, voluntary hyperventilation, and breath-holding.

questions.text: Define the breaking point of a breath-holding test.
questions.explanation: Hyperventilation delays the breaking point mainly by lowering starting PCO₂, whereas breathing oxygen alone has a smaller effect on this CO₂-driven limit.
questions.keyConcept: Rising CO₂, more than falling O₂, usually determines the breath-holding breaking point.
questions.modelAnswer: The breaking point is the moment when accumulating CO₂ and H⁺ generate a respiratory drive strong enough to overcome voluntary inhibition, forcing breathing to resume.

questions.text: Define acclimatization to high altitude.
questions.explanation: These changes compensate for low inspired PO₂ over days to weeks; renal bicarbonate loss is crucial because it permits continued hyperventilation despite respiratory alkalosis.
questions.keyConcept: Major adaptations include sustained hyperventilation, renal bicarbonate loss, increased erythropoietin and red-cell mass, increased 2,3-DPG, and tissue-level changes.
questions.modelAnswer: Acclimatization is the progressive set of physiologic adaptations that improves oxygen uptake and delivery during prolonged exposure to low barometric pressure and hypoxia at high altitude.

questions.text: Define stagnant (circulatory) hypoxia.
questions.explanation: Oxygen delivery equals blood flow multiplied by arterial oxygen content; therefore, low flow alone can cause tissue hypoxia even when the blood leaving the lungs is normally oxygenated.
questions.keyConcept: The primary defect is perfusion, not pulmonary oxygenation or hemoglobin concentration.
questions.modelAnswer: Stagnant hypoxia is inadequate tissue oxygen delivery caused by reduced blood flow, despite normal arterial PO₂ and often normal arterial oxygen content.

questions.text: Define hyperbaric oxygen therapy.
questions.explanation: This is useful when hemoglobin-dependent delivery is compromised, such as carbon monoxide poisoning, and in selected ischemic or anaerobic infections, but it also increases oxygen-toxicity and barotrauma risks.
questions.keyConcept: Hyperbaric pressure greatly increases physically dissolved oxygen in plasma beyond what normobaric oxygen can achieve.
questions.modelAnswer: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is administration of 100% oxygen at an ambient pressure greater than one atmosphere absolute in a sealed chamber.

questions.text: Discuss the sneezing reflex.
questions.explanation: Unlike cough, which primarily follows lower-airway irritation, sneeze begins in nasal mucosa and preferentially directs the clearing airflow through the nose.
questions.keyConcept: Sneezing is a trigeminally triggered protective reflex that clears the nasal cavity by explosive expiratory airflow.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Irritation of the nasal mucosa activates trigeminal afferents.
- A deep inspiration is followed by forceful expiration, with airflow directed mainly through the nose.
- The explosive airflow expels mucus, particles, and irritants from the nasal passages.

questions.text: Define the gut protective respiratory reflexes.
questions.explanation: The airway and digestive tract share the pharynx; temporarily pausing ventilation and sealing the laryngeal inlet prevents material from being inhaled during transit.
questions.keyConcept: Deglutition apnea and glottic closure coordinate breathing with swallowing to prevent aspiration.
questions.modelAnswer: During swallowing and vomiting, breathing is briefly inhibited and the glottis closes to prevent food or vomitus from entering the respiratory tract.

questions.text: Discuss the changes in ventilation during muscular exercise.
questions.explanation: This two-phase response explains why ventilation begins rising before blood gases change substantially, then remains elevated afterward while metabolic and thermal disturbances resolve.
questions.keyConcept: Exercise ventilation has an early neural phase and a later metabolic phase, allowing gas exchange to track changing muscle demand.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Ventilation rises abruptly at exercise onset because of central command and proprioceptor input.
- It then increases more gradually as metabolic CO₂ production, H⁺, temperature, and other chemical signals rise.
- During strenuous exercise, both tidal volume and respiratory rate increase.
- After exercise, ventilation falls rapidly at first and then more slowly during recovery.

questions.text: What is the prosthetic group of the NADH dehydrogenase complex?
questions.explanation: FMN is the initial prosthetic electron acceptor in Complex I. In contrast, FAD is a bound flavin cofactor rather than the principal soluble acceptor in glycolysis.

questions.text: Coenzyme Q and cytochrome c are mobile electron carriers in the respiratory chain.
questions.explanation: Coenzyme Q diffuses within the lipid core of the inner membrane and carries electrons to Complex III. Cytochrome c is a soluble peripheral protein that moves along the outer membrane surface from Complex III to Complex IV, so the statement is true.

questions.text: Cytochrome b is a protein containing which prosthetic group?

questions.text: Which compound is an uncoupler of oxidative phosphorylation?

questions.text: Ubiquinone is the only nonprotein member of the electron transport chain.

questions.text: Complete the statements about cellular respiration, glycolysis, pyruvate dehydrogenase, and mitochondrial shuttles.
questions.explanation: The reasoning connects “Cellular respiration uses oxygen to oxidize fuels to carbon dioxide and water and generates most cellular ATP” to “Glycolysis converts one glucose to two pyruvate and two cytosolic NADH.” That sequence is the mechanism, comparison, or anatomical relationship being tested in the statements about cellular respiration, glycolysis, pyruvate dehydrogenase, and mitochondrial shuttles.
questions.keyConcept: Cellular respiration generate ATP using O2 in oxidation of fuels to CO2 and water • Cellular respiration uses over 90% of the inhaled O₂• • The complete oxidation of the acetyl group to CO2 occurs in the tricarboxylic ac
questions.modelAnswer:
- Cellular respiration uses oxygen to oxidize fuels to carbon dioxide and water and generates most cellular ATP.
- Glycolysis converts one glucose to two pyruvate and two cytosolic NADH.
- Pyruvate is oxidatively decarboxylated by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex to acetyl-CoA, and the TCA cycle oxidizes acetyl units while producing NADH and FADH2.
- The respiratory chain is in the inner mitochondrial membrane, whereas most TCA-cycle enzymes are in the matrix.
- Cytosolic NADH reducing equivalents enter through the malate-aspartate or glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle.
- Pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase is inhibited by ADP and pyruvate and activated by ATP, acetyl-CoA, and NADH; pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase is activated by Ca2+.
- Arsenite inhibits lipoate-dependent complexes, including pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.

questions.text: What are the three phases of cellular respiration?
questions.explanation: Fuel oxidation first converges on acetyl-CoA, respiratory electron transfer then captures that energy as ATP, and ATP hydrolysis finally powers cellular work. Separating these phases clarifies that oxygen is consumed by the respiratory chain rather than directly by glycolysis.
questions.keyConcept: Oxidation of fuels (carbohydrates, lipids and proteins).
questions.modelAnswer: Phase 1 oxidizes carbohydrates, fatty acids, and amino acids to acetyl-CoA. Phase 2 oxidizes acetyl-CoA and transfers electrons from NADH and FADH2 through the respiratory chain to oxygen while generating ATP. Phase 3 uses ATP hydrolysis to drive energy-requiring cellular processes.

questions.text: Explain phase 2 of cellular respiration.
questions.explanation: NADH and FADH2 are oxidized only when their electrons can move to oxygen through the respiratory chain. Proton pumping stores the released redox energy as a gradient, which ATP synthase converts into phosphoryl-transfer energy.
questions.keyConcept: Electrons are transferred from NADH and FADH2 to O2 by the electron transport chain (ETC).
questions.modelAnswer: NADH and FADH2 donate electrons to the respiratory chain, which ultimately reduces oxygen to water. Electron transfer pumps protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, and ATP synthase uses the proton-motive force to form ATP.

questions.text: Why are mitochondria the main site of cellular respiration?
